title: MODULE 05 — Modern JavaScript for Web Applications

overview.text: This module introduces the programming foundation of modern frontend engineering.
In the previous modules, students learned how the web works, how to structure HTML documents, how to engineer CSS layouts, and how to build responsive and accessible interfaces.
Now they will learn how to make those interfaces actually work.

JavaScript enables websites to respond to user actions, manipulate document content, process data, communicate with external services, manage application state, and implement complex application behavior.
The objective is to move beyond writing small scripts and develop the ability to design, understand, debug, and maintain JavaScript applications.
Learning Outcomes
By completing this module, students should be able to:
Understand JavaScript engines, runtimes, execution contexts, and the event loop.
Understand variables, primitive types, reference types, and type conversions.
Write conditional logic, loops, and iteration-based programs.
Develop reusable functions and understand lexical scope and closures.
Manipulate arrays and objects using modern JavaScript methods.
Apply destructuring, spread, rest, and modern language syntax.
Organize applications using ECMAScript modules.
Manipulate the DOM and respond to browser events.
Understand event propagation, capturing, bubbling, and delegation.
Handle errors and debug applications using browser developer tools.
Apply object-oriented and functional programming techniques.
Understand JavaScript memory management and performance considerations.
Build an interactive application using vanilla JavaScript without a frontend framework.
Module Overview
Develop the programming skills needed to build dynamic interfaces.

JavaScript is a high-level programming language widely used to develop interactive web applications. It allows developers to execute application logic in browsers, manipulate HTML documents, handle user interactions, process data, and communicate with backend services.

Modern JavaScript engineering requires more than knowing variables and writing functions. Developers must understand how JavaScript executes, how values are stored and manipulated, how scope works, how asynchronous operations are handled, how browser events propagate, and how application code should be organized.
This module builds these abilities progressively, beginning with JavaScript execution fundamentals and advancing toward application architecture, debugging, programming patterns, and performance.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — JavaScript Runtime and Execution Fundamentals

blocks.text: JavaScript is a high-level, dynamically typed, multi-paradigm programming language.
It supports several programming approaches, including:
JavaScript is one of the core technologies used to develop modern web applications.
HTML defines the structure of a page.
JavaScript defines its behavior and application logic.
For example, consider a course registration button.
const button = document.querySelector("#enrolButton"); button.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Course enrolment initiated."); });
When the user clicks the button, JavaScript responds to the browser event and executes the callback.
This is an example of event-driven programming.
These terms are related but not identical.
ECMAScript is the standardized language specification that defines JavaScript's core language behavior.
JavaScript refers to implementations of the ECMAScript language, together with the APIs and runtime environments in which it executes.
For example, a browser provides APIs that JavaScript can use:
These browser APIs are not all part of the ECMAScript language specification itself.
This distinction becomes important when JavaScript runs in different environments.
A JavaScript engine is software that processes and executes JavaScript code.
V8 — used by Chromium-based browsers and Node.js.
An engine is responsible for tasks such as:
Different engines have different internal implementations, but they implement the JavaScript language according to the applicable standards.
A JavaScript runtime provides the environment in which JavaScript code executes.
For browser JavaScript, the browser provides capabilities such as:
For Node.js, the runtime provides different APIs, including:
This explains why some JavaScript code works in browsers but fails in Node.js.
This code requires a DOM environment.
A regular Node.js process does not automatically provide the browser's document object.
const price = 100; const tax = 10; const total = price + tax; console.log(total);
When this code executes, the JavaScript engine must:
Modern engines may combine interpretation, compilation, and runtime optimization rather than executing every instruction through one simple mechanism.
An execution context is an internal structure associated with JavaScript code execution.
It provides the environment required to execute statements, resolve identifiers, and access variables and functions.
This is created when JavaScript begins executing a script or applicable module environment.
const websiteName = "PrepSpaces"; function displayWebsite() { console.log(websiteName); } displayWebsite();
The top-level code executes within its relevant global or module execution environment.
A browser also provides a global environment associated with globalThis.
A function execution context is created when a function is invoked.
function calculateTotal(price, tax) { const total = price + tax; return total; } const result = calculateTotal(100, 10);
When calculateTotal() is called, its execution has access to:
JavaScript also defines an execution context associated with eval() evaluation.
Direct eval() has special scope behavior and can create difficult optimization and security problems.
Avoid using eval() for ordinary application development.
The call stack tracks active JavaScript function execution.
function first() { second(); } function second() { third(); } function third() { console.log("Execution complete"); } first();
The execution proceeds through function calls.
Conceptually, the call stack develops as follows:
Call first() │ ├── first() │ │ │ └── second() │ │ │ └── third() │ └── Functions return
The innermost function normally completes before control returns to its caller.
This is known as last-in, first-out behavior.
A stack overflow can occur when function calls continue growing without returning.
Eventually, the engine reaches an implementation-dependent call-stack limit and throws an error, commonly a RangeError.
A recursive function must have an appropriate termination condition.
function countdown(number) { if (number <= 0) { return; } console.log(number); countdown(number - 1); } countdown(5);
JavaScript uses lexical environments to resolve variable and function names.
const platform = "PrepSpaces"; function display() { const course = "Frontend Engineering"; console.log(platform); console.log(course); } display();
The function can access platform from its surrounding environment.
However, code outside the function cannot normally access the local course binding.
This is one of the foundations of lexical scope, which is explored in greater depth in Lesson 04.
Each statement executes in the current execution flow.
A long-running synchronous operation can prevent other work on the same JavaScript thread, including browser interactions and rendering tasks that need that thread.
Some operations do not need to block the current execution flow while waiting for their results.
File and database operations in supported environments.
The timer callback does not immediately execute at the position where setTimeout() appears.
The browser manages the timer through its host environment and schedules the callback when it becomes eligible for execution.
The event loop coordinates asynchronous execution in JavaScript environments.
The browser can manage operations such as timers and network activity outside the immediate synchronous JavaScript execution.
When callbacks become eligible, the event loop coordinates when they can execute.
The important concept is that asynchronous operations can be completed or made ready without blocking the current JavaScript call stack continuously.
Tasks may originate from activities such as:
After the current JavaScript execution finishes, the environment processes pending microtasks according to its event-loop rules.
In browsers, rendering opportunities and other event-loop processing occur according to the HTML event-loop model.
console.log("Start"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Timer"); }, 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log("Promise"); }); console.log("End");
The timer callback is scheduled as a task.
The promise reaction is scheduled as a microtask.
The current synchronous JavaScript execution finishes.
The timer task runs when the event loop reaches it.
A zero-millisecond timer does not mean that its callback executes immediately.
JavaScript interacts with the browser's rendering process.
The browser updates the relevant document styling and performs the rendering work required to show the change.
Large synchronous JavaScript tasks can block the main thread and delay:
Understanding this relationship is important for building responsive applications.
Web Workers allow certain JavaScript operations to execute on separate worker threads.
They are useful for computational work that would otherwise block the main browser thread.
const worker = new Worker("worker.js"); worker.postMessage(1000000); worker.addEventListener("message", (event) => { console.log("Result:", event.data); });
The worker communicates with the main script through messages.
A standard dedicated worker does not directly access the document DOM.
They are not a replacement for the main JavaScript environment when DOM manipulation is required.
A recursive function with a termination condition.
Use the browser Console and Performance tools to observe execution.

sections.title: LESSON 02 — Variables, Data Types and Operators

blocks.text: A variable is a named binding used to refer to a value.
Variables allow programs to store and manipulate information.
const courseName = "Frontend Engineering"; let studentCount = 100; console.log(courseName); console.log(studentCount);
courseName refers to a string value.
studentCount refers to a number value.
JavaScript is dynamically typed, which means variable bindings are not permanently restricted to one declared type.
JavaScript provides three commonly used variable declaration keywords.

var
var is the older variable declaration mechanism.
var username = "Alex"; var username = "Sam"; console.log(username);
var allows redeclaration within the same scope.
It is function-scoped or global-scoped depending on where it is declared.
It also has behavior associated with hoisting.
The value can change, but the same binding cannot be redeclared within the same lexical scope.
This does not mean that every value referenced by a const binding is completely immutable.
This works because the object is mutated without reassigning the student binding.
causes an error because the binding cannot be reassigned.
Prefer const when reassignment is unnecessary.
Use let when a binding needs to change.
Avoid introducing var in modern application code unless maintaining older code or understanding legacy behavior.
const name = "Alex"; const course = 'JavaScript'; const message = `Welcome to ${course}`;
const age = 22; const price = 4999.99; const percentage = 85;
JavaScript uses the Number type for most ordinary numeric values.
It follows IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point representation.
The result is commonly represented as:
For financial calculations, consider storing monetary values in the smallest integer unit, such as paise, where the application requirements permit it.
BigInt represents integers larger than the safe integer range of Number.
BigInt values use the n suffix for numeric literals.
BigInt and Number cannot generally be mixed directly in arithmetic operations without explicit conversion.
const isLoggedIn = true; const hasCompletedCourse = false;
Boolean values are used extensively in conditions and state management.
Represents a value that has not been assigned.
It can also occur when accessing a missing object property:
Represents an intentional absence of a value.
This is a long-standing language behavior and does not mean null is actually an object.
Symbol creates a unique primitive value.
const id = Symbol("student"); const anotherId = Symbol("student"); console.log(id === anotherId);
Symbols are useful for unique property keys and certain advanced programming patterns.
Objects and functions are reference-type values.
The variable refers to an object value.
Two different variables may refer to the same object.
const first = { name: "Alex" }; const second = first; second.name = "Sam"; console.log(first.name);
Both bindings refer to the same object.
This is an important foundation for understanding mutation and object copying.
The typeof operator identifies the type category of a value.

console.log(typeof "Hello"); console.log(typeof 100); console.log(typeof true); console.log(typeof undefined); console.log(typeof 100n); console.log(typeof Symbol()); console.log(typeof {}); console.log(typeof function () {});
string number boolean undefined bigint symbol object function
const a = 10; const b = 3; console.log(a + b); console.log(a - b); console.log(a * b); console.log(a / b); console.log(a % b); console.log(a ** b);
let score = 10; score += 5; score -= 2; score *= 3; score /= 2;
These combine assignment and another operation.
Returns true because type coercion occurs.
Returns false because the types differ.
Prefer strict equality in most application code.
Strict inequality does not perform the same type conversion used by loose inequality.
&& returns the first falsy operand or the final operand if all operands are truthy.
|| returns the first truthy operand or the final operand if all operands are falsy.
! converts its operand to Boolean and negates the result.
?? returns the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined.
This differs from ||, which also treats values such as 0, false, and "" as falsy.
JavaScript evaluates values as truthy or falsy in Boolean contexts.
Other values, including empty arrays and empty objects, are truthy.
The condition is truthy because an array is an object value.
JavaScript can convert values between types.
const number = Number("100"); const text = String(250); const boolean = Boolean(1);
JavaScript may convert values automatically during operations.
The string concatenation behavior is applied.
The subtraction operation converts the string to a number.
Implicit conversion is sometimes called type coercion.
It represents an invalid numerical result.
This checks whether the supplied value is specifically the numeric NaN value.
Parentheses can make the intended operation explicit:
Use parentheses when an expression becomes difficult to read.
The conditional or ternary operator provides a compact conditional expression.
Use it for simple conditional value selection.
Complex business logic is generally clearer with regular if...else statements.
Declare variables using const and let.
Store information about students and courses.
Use nullish coalescing to provide default values.
Explain the difference between falsy and empty values.
Control flow defines the order in which program statements execute.
Without control-flow structures, a program would generally execute statements sequentially.
JavaScript provides structures that allow programs to make decisions, repeat operations, and respond to different conditions.

if
else
else if
switch
for
while
do...while
for...of
for...in
The if statement executes code when a condition evaluates to truthy.
The block runs because the condition is true.
Use else to execute an alternative block.
const score = 35; if (score >= 50) { console.log("Passed"); } else { console.log("Failed"); }
Multiple conditions can be evaluated sequentially.
const score = 85; if (score >= 90) { console.log("Excellent"); } else if (score >= 75) { console.log("Very Good"); } else if (score >= 50) { console.log("Passed"); } else { console.log("Failed"); }
The first matching condition determines the executed branch.
For example, placing score >= 50 before score >= 90 would prevent the more specific higher-score branches from running.
Conditions can appear inside other conditions.
const isLoggedIn = true; const hasAccess = true; if (isLoggedIn) { if (hasAccess) { console.log("Access granted"); } else { console.log("Access denied"); } } else { console.log("Please log in"); }
For complex logic, consider combining conditions or extracting functions to improve readability.
A switch statement evaluates an expression and matches its value against case clauses.

const role = "student"; switch (role) { case "admin": console.log("Administrator dashboard"); break; case "student": console.log("Student dashboard"); break; case "instructor": console.log("Instructor dashboard"); break; default: console.log("Unknown role"); }
The break statement prevents execution from falling through to subsequent cases.
Sometimes fall-through behavior is intentional, but it should be deliberate and clearly documented.
Switch uses strict matching for its case values.
A for loop repeats a block using initialization, a condition, and an update expression.
for ( let i = 0; i < 5; i++ ) { console.log(i); }
The loop ends when the condition becomes false.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains truthy.
A while loop is useful when the number of iterations is not necessarily known in advance.
Always ensure that an appropriate termination condition exists.
A do...while loop executes its body before checking the condition.
let count = 0; do { console.log(count); count++; } while (count < 5);
This guarantees at least one execution of the loop body.
const courses = [ "Frontend", "Backend", "Data Engineering" ]; for (const course of courses) { console.log(course); }
for...in iterates over enumerable string property keys of an object, including inherited enumerable properties.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22, course: "JavaScript" }; for (const key in student) { console.log(key, student[key]); }
For arrays, for...in is usually not the preferred iteration method because it iterates keys rather than values and may include additional enumerable properties.
Use for...of or array iteration methods for normal array-value processing.
break terminates the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement.
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i === 5) { break; } console.log(i); }
The loop stops when i reaches 5.
continue skips the remainder of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next iteration when appropriate.
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { if (i === 3) { continue; } console.log(i); }
A loop can exist inside another loop.
for (let row = 1; row <= 3; row++) { for (let column = 1; column <= 3; column++) { console.log(row, column); } }
However, nested loops can become expensive when processing large datasets.
3.15 Conditional Logic With Real Application Data

const tasks = [ { title: "Learn HTML", completed: true }, { title: "Learn CSS", completed: true }, { title: "Learn JavaScript", completed: false } ]; for (const task of tasks) { if (task.completed) { console.log(task.title, "Completed"); } else { console.log(task.title, "Pending"); } }
This demonstrates how control flow processes structured application information.
Repeat while a condition remains true
Execute a callback for array elements
The choice depends on whether you need an index, iterable values, early termination, or other loop control.
Find a value in a collection.
Stop processing when a condition is satisfied.
Generate a report using conditional logic.
A function is a reusable block of JavaScript code designed to perform a specific operation.
Functions help developers organize logic and avoid unnecessary duplication.
function greet() { console.log("Welcome to PrepSpaces"); } greet();
The function is defined once and can be invoked whenever necessary.
Parameters are named inputs defined by a function.
Arguments are the actual values supplied when calling it.
function calculateTotal(price, tax) { return price + tax; } const total = calculateTotal(100, 10); console.log(total);
The result becomes available to the calling code.
A function without an explicit return statement returns undefined.
A function declaration defines a named function.
function calculateArea(width, height) { return width * height; }
Function declarations are initialized during the relevant environment's declaration-instantiation process and can generally be called before their declaration appears in the source code.
console.log(add(5, 10)); function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
A function can be assigned to a variable.
const calculateArea = function(width, height) { return width * height; };
The function expression is created when execution reaches the assignment.
The variable binding rules depend on whether it was declared with const, let, or another mechanism.
Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax for function expressions.
const add = (a, b) => { return a + b; };
For a single expression, they can use implicit return:
An important distinction: arrow functions do not create their own this, arguments, or super bindings. They use surrounding lexical behavior where applicable.
Default parameters provide fallback values when arguments are omitted or undefined.
An explicitly supplied null does not activate the default value.
Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array.
function calculateTotal(...prices) { return prices.reduce( (total, price) => total + price, 0 ); } console.log(calculateTotal(100, 200, 300));
The prices parameter is an array.
Only one rest parameter is permitted, and it must appear last in the parameter list.
function executeOperation(operation, a, b) { return operation(a, b); } function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } console.log(executeOperation(multiply, 5, 4));
This is the foundation of callback-based programming.
A higher-order function accepts another function as an argument, returns a function, or both.
function createMultiplier(multiplier) { return function(number) { return number * multiplier; }; } const double = createMultiplier(2); console.log(double(10));
This returns a function that multiplies numbers by two.
Scope determines where variable bindings can be accessed.
JavaScript has several important scope concepts.
A binding declared in the global environment may be accessible throughout relevant parts of the script or environment.
The exact behavior of top-level declarations differs between classic browser scripts and ECMAScript modules.
Variables declared with var inside a function are function-scoped.
The variable cannot normally be accessed outside the function.

let and const create block-scoped bindings.
if (true) { const message = "Inside block"; console.log(message); }
The message variable is not accessible outside its block.
Lexical scope means that variable access is determined by where functions and blocks are written in the source code.
const platform = "PrepSpaces"; function outer() { const course = "JavaScript"; function inner() { console.log(platform); console.log(course); } inner(); } outer();
The inner function can access bindings from its surrounding lexical environments.
When JavaScript encounters a variable name, it looks for a matching binding in the relevant lexical environment.
If it cannot find the binding locally, it checks the enclosing environment.
This lookup continues through the scope chain.

const globalMessage = "Global"; function first() { const firstMessage = "First"; function second() { const secondMessage = "Second"; console.log(globalMessage); console.log(firstMessage); console.log(secondMessage); } second(); } first();
The innermost function can access all three values.
Hoisting describes how declarations are processed during environment initialization before normal statement execution.
A var binding is created and initialized with undefined during declaration processing.
These bindings are created during environment initialization but remain uninitialized until the declaration is evaluated.
Accessing them before initialization causes a ReferenceError.
The period between scope entry and binding initialization is called the temporal dead zone.
Function declarations are generally initialized before ordinary statement execution within their applicable declaration scope.
A closure occurs when a function retains access to its surrounding lexical environment, even after the outer function has finished executing.
function createCounter() { let count = 0; return function() { count++; return count; }; } const counter = createCounter(); console.log(counter()); console.log(counter()); console.log(counter());
The returned function retains access to count.
This allows state to remain private within the closure.

function createCourseTracker(courseName) { let completedLessons = 0; return { completeLesson() { completedLessons++; }, getProgress(totalLessons) { return ( completedLessons / totalLessons ) * 100; }, getCourseName() { return courseName; } }; } const frontendCourse = createCourseTracker("Frontend Engineering"); frontendCourse.completeLesson(); frontendCourse.completeLesson(); console.log( frontendCourse.getProgress(10) );
The internal counter is not directly exposed.
Closures preserve access to their referenced lexical environment.
This can be useful, but it also means developers should consider object lifetimes.
If a long-lived function retains references to a large object that is no longer needed, that object may remain reachable.
Understanding closures helps when investigating unexpected memory retention.
this refers to a value determined by the function's execution context.
const student = { name: "Alex", greet() { console.log(this.name); } }; student.greet();
In this method call, this refers to the student object.
However, this behaves differently depending on invocation.
In strict mode, a normal standalone function call generally has undefined as its this value.
In non-strict classic scripts, it can refer to the global object in certain situations.
Arrow functions use the surrounding lexical this rather than receiving their own function-specific this.
The detailed application of this is explored further in Lesson 11.
Explain hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
Create a private counter using closures.
Build a course progress tracker using closures.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — Arrays, Objects and Data Manipulation

blocks.text: An array is an object used to store an ordered collection of values.
Arrays can be created using array literals.
They can also be created with the Array constructor, although literals are generally clearer.
Array values can contain different types:
However, predictable data structures are usually easier to maintain in real applications.
The length property returns the number of elements.
Adds one or more items to the end.
These methods mutate the original array.
Returns a shallow copy of a selected portion.
const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; const selected = numbers.slice(1, 4); console.log(selected);
Can remove, replace, or insert elements at particular positions.
const courses = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"]; for (let i = 0; i < courses.length; i++) { console.log(courses[i]); }
forEach() executes a callback for each array element.
It does not create a transformed array and does not support ordinary early termination using break.
map() creates a new array by transforming each element.
const prices = [100, 200, 300]; const increasedPrices = prices.map(price => { return price * 1.1; }); console.log(increasedPrices);
The original array is not modified by the mapping operation itself.
filter() creates a new array containing elements that pass a condition.
const scores = [40, 85, 60, 30, 95]; const passed = scores.filter(score => { return score >= 50; });
Use it to implement filtering for:
reduce() processes array values and accumulates a result.
const prices = [100, 200, 300]; const total = prices.reduce( (sum, price) => sum + price, 0 ); console.log(total);
The second argument is the initial accumulator value.
However, do not use reduce when a simpler map, filter, or loop makes the logic easier to understand.
find() returns the first matching element.
const courses = [ { id: 1, name: "HTML" }, { id: 2, name: "CSS" }, { id: 3, name: "JavaScript" } ]; const selected = courses.find( course => course.id === 2 );
findIndex() returns the index of the first matching element.
Both return an appropriate not-found result when no matching element exists.
every() checks whether all elements pass a condition.
const scores = [80, 90, 85]; const allPassed = scores.every( score => score >= 50 );
some() checks whether at least one element passes a condition.
const scores = [20, 30, 85]; const someonePassed = scores.some( score => score >= 50 );
For numbers, provide a comparison function:
const numbers = [40, 5, 100, 25]; numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b);
Modern ECMAScript requires stable sorting behavior for Array.prototype.sort.
To avoid mutating the original array, copy it before sorting:
Modern JavaScript also supports non-mutating alternatives such as toSorted() in supported environments.
An object stores information using key-value properties.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22, course: "JavaScript", isEnrolled: true };
Objects are central to representing application data.
Bracket notation is useful when property names contain spaces or when the key is determined dynamically.
Objects can be modified after creation unless they have been restricted through mechanisms such as Object.freeze().
const student = { name: "Alex", course: { title: "Frontend Engineering", duration: "Six Months" } }; console.log(student.course.title);
This is useful for modelling structured application data.
A common application data structure is an array of objects.
const tasks = [ { id: 1, title: "Learn HTML", completed: true }, { id: 2, title: "Learn CSS", completed: true }, { id: 3, title: "Learn JavaScript", completed: false } ];
This structure is useful for displaying, searching, filtering, and updating application records.
An object can contain functions as property values.
const student = { name: "Alex", greet() { return `Hello, ${this.name}`; } }; console.log(student.greet());
The function is called a method when used as an object property in this way.
JavaScript properties contain metadata describing their behavior.
const student = { name: "Alex" }; const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(student, "name"); console.log(descriptor);
These provide greater control over object properties.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22, course: "JavaScript" }; console.log(Object.keys(student)); console.log(Object.values(student)); console.log(Object.entries(student));
These methods return collections describing an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties.
They are useful for object inspection and transformation.
const original = { name: "Alex" }; const copy = original; copy.name = "Sam"; console.log(original.name);
Both variables refer to the same object.
const original = { name: "Alex", address: { city: "Nagpur" } }; const copy = { ...original }; copy.address.city = "Mumbai"; console.log(original.address.city);
The original nested object is also modified.
This is because the copy is shallow.
Deep copying requires a deliberate strategy.
structuredClone() has defined limitations, including certain unsupported values such as functions.
JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation.
It is a widely used text-based format for exchanging structured data.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22 }; const json = JSON.stringify(student);
Convert JSON back into a JavaScript value:
JSON is commonly used in API communication and browser storage.
Undefined object properties are generally omitted.
Circular references cannot be serialized directly.
JSON data does not preserve every JavaScript object type.
A Map stores key-value pairs and can use values of different types as keys.
const courses = new Map(); courses.set(1, "HTML"); courses.set(2, "CSS"); console.log(courses.get(1));
const skills = new Set(); skills.add("HTML"); skills.add("CSS"); skills.add("HTML"); console.log(skills);
Only one instance of each equal value is stored.
Sets are useful for deduplication and membership checks.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — Destructuring, Spread and Rest Operators

blocks.text: Destructuring is a JavaScript syntax that allows values to be extracted from arrays or objects and assigned to variables.
It makes data access more readable.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22, course: "JavaScript" }; const name = student.name; const age = student.age;
This creates bindings using the specified object properties.
const courses = [ "HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript" ]; const [first, second, third] = courses; console.log(first); console.log(second); console.log(third);
Array destructuring works based on position.
You can skip elements using empty positions.
const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]; const [first, , third] = numbers; console.log(first); console.log(third);
Destructuring can provide default values when a corresponding value is undefined.
const student = { name: "Alex" }; const { name, age = 18 } = student; console.log(age);
The value becomes 18 because age is undefined.
A property explicitly containing null does not activate the default.
You can assign an object property to a variable with a different name.
const student = { name: "Alex", course: "JavaScript" }; const { name: studentName, course: courseName } = student;
This is useful when multiple objects contain similarly named properties or a clearer local name is required.
const student = { name: "Alex", course: { title: "Frontend Engineering", level: "Intermediate" } }; const { course: { title, level } } = student;
Nested destructuring is useful for structured data, but excessive nesting can make code difficult to read.
Functions can destructure object parameters directly.
function displayCourse({ title, level }) { console.log(title); console.log(level); } displayCourse({ title: "Frontend Engineering", level: "Intermediate" });
This is commonly used in modern application code and component APIs.
When a parameter itself may be missing, provide an appropriate default object or validate it before destructuring.
The spread syntax expands an iterable or enumerable object properties into another context, depending on where it is used.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22 }; const updatedStudent = { ...student, course: "JavaScript" };
The original properties are copied into a new object, followed by the additional property.
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22 }; const updated = { ...student, age: 23 };
The later age property overrides the earlier one.
Reversing the order would allow the original age property to override the later value.
const frontend = ["HTML", "CSS"]; const backend = ["Java", "SQL"]; const technologies = [ ...frontend, ...backend ];
Spread can also pass iterable values as individual arguments.
The array values are passed as separate arguments.
Rest syntax collects remaining items into a new array or object, depending on the context.
function calculateTotal(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce( (total, number) => total + number, 0 ); }
The rest parameter collects all remaining function arguments.
const courses = [ "HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript", "React" ]; const [first, second, ...remaining] = courses; console.log(remaining);
const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22, course: "JavaScript", city: "Nagpur" }; const { name, ...otherDetails } = student;
The rest property collects the remaining enumerable own properties that were not selected.
The syntax looks the same, but the operation depends on the context.
Optional chaining safely accesses properties or calls functions when an intermediate value may be nullish.
If an intermediate value is null or undefined, the expression short-circuits to undefined.
It is useful when handling partially populated API data.
The nullish coalescing operator provides a default when a value is null or undefined.
The logical OR version also replaces valid falsy values such as an empty string.
Extracts student information using object destructuring.
Extracts course values using array destructuring.
Uses spread to copy arrays and objects.
Uses rest properties to separate object data.
Uses optional chaining for nested API-style objects.
Uses nullish coalescing for default display values.
Demonstrates the difference between shallow and deep copying.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — Modern JavaScript Features and ES Modules

blocks.text: Modern JavaScript refers to the language features and programming techniques used in contemporary JavaScript applications.
ECMAScript has evolved over time, introducing features that help developers write more readable, maintainable, and expressive code.
These features reduce unnecessary complexity and improve application organization.
They allow expressions to be embedded directly into strings.
const name = "Alex"; const course = "JavaScript"; const message = `Welcome ${name}, you are learning ${course}.`; console.log(message);
Template literals also support multiple lines.
const message = ` Welcome to PrepSpaces. Start learning JavaScript today. `;
Modern JavaScript allows more concise object definitions.
const name = "Alex"; const age = 22; const student = { name, age };
This is equivalent to assigning the corresponding property names explicitly.
Object property names can be calculated using expressions.
The resulting object contains a property named course.
These operators are important when working with uncertain application data.
The optional chaining operator prevents a property-access error when an intermediate object is nullish.
The nullish coalescing operator provides a fallback when the final result is nullish.
A Promise represents the eventual outcome of an asynchronous operation.
const result = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const success = true; if (success) { resolve("Operation completed"); } else { reject(new Error("Operation failed")); } });
A promise can be handled using:
then() handles fulfillment and can also handle rejection through its second callback argument.

catch() handles rejection.
finally() runs after the promise settles, regardless of outcome.
Async and await provide a more straightforward way to write asynchronous JavaScript.

async function loadCourses() { try { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Failed to load courses"); } const courses = await response.json(); console.log(courses); } catch (error) { console.error(error); } } loadCourses();
An async function always returns a Promise.
await pauses the continuation of that async function until the awaited Promise settles, without blocking the entire JavaScript thread.
Important: fetch() generally rejects on network failures, but an HTTP error status such as 404 or 500 does not automatically reject the Promise. Check response.ok or the status explicitly.

Promise.all() waits for all supplied promises to fulfill.
async function loadDashboard() { const [courses, progress, profile] = await Promise.all([ fetch("/api/courses").then(r => r.json()), fetch("/api/progress").then(r => r.json()), fetch("/api/profile").then(r => r.json()) ]); console.log(courses, progress, profile); }
If any input promise rejects, the returned Promise rejects.
This is useful when several independent resources are needed.

Promise.allSettled() waits for all supplied promises to settle.
const results = await Promise.allSettled([ fetch("/api/courses"), fetch("/api/profile"), fetch("/api/progress") ]);
It returns the outcome of each promise rather than rejecting immediately because one failed.

Promise.race() settles with the outcome of the first input promise to settle.
Promise.any() fulfills with the first fulfilled input promise, or rejects with an AggregateError when all inputs reject.
These methods support different asynchronous coordination strategies.
Modules organize JavaScript into separate files with explicit imports and exports.
Modules are a core part of modern JavaScript applications.
A module can export multiple named values.
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; } export function subtract(a, b) { return a - b; }
import { add, subtract } from "./math.js"; console.log(add(10, 5)); console.log(subtract(10, 5));
A module can provide a default export.
export default class User { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } }
import User from "./user.js"; const student = new User("Alex");
A module can have one default export.
This is useful when avoiding naming conflicts or clarifying usage.
A module can re-export values from other modules.
This supports organized module entry points.
For larger applications, developers may create an index module that exposes the public API of a component or feature folder.
This tells the browser to load the script as an ECMAScript module.
They generally need to be served through an appropriate HTTP server rather than relying on direct file:// access.
Dynamic imports allow modules to be loaded when needed.
async function openReports() { const reports = await import("./reports.js"); reports.displayReports(); }
In supported ECMAScript module environments, await can be used directly at the module's top level.
const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); const courses = await response.json(); console.log(courses);
This is module-level behavior, not a general feature of ordinary classic scripts.
Modern JavaScript includes many useful standard library methods.

Array.prototype.toSorted()
const numbers = [5, 2, 9]; const sorted = numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);
Creates a sorted copy rather than modifying the original array.

Object.fromEntries()
const entries = [ ["name", "Alex"], ["course", "JavaScript"] ]; const student = Object.fromEntries(entries);
Converts entry pairs into an object.
Checks whether a string contains another string.
Checks whether a string begins with a specified value.
These methods should be used according to the project's supported browser targets.
A larger application may separate code according to responsibility.
src/ │ ├── data/ │ └── courses.js │ ├── services/ │ └── courseService.js │ ├── utils/ │ └── formatDate.js │ ├── components/ │ └── courseCard.js │ └── main.js
Each module should have a clear responsibility.
Avoid creating a single enormous JavaScript file containing every feature.
Create a multi-file JavaScript application containing:
Run the application using a local development server.

sections.title: LESSON 08 — DOM Manipulation and Event Handling

blocks.text: DOM stands for Document Object Model.
It is a programming interface that represents an HTML document as a structured tree of nodes and objects.
The browser constructs the DOM when it parses HTML.
JavaScript can access and modify this structure.
The browser creates a corresponding DOM structure.
JavaScript can then inspect and modify it.
The DOM API provides several methods for finding elements.
Selects an element by its ID.
Returns a static NodeList of matching elements.
Understanding the difference between live collections and static NodeLists can help prevent iteration and update problems.
textContent treats the supplied value as text rather than parsing it as HTML.
This makes it a useful and generally safer choice when displaying untrusted content.
innerHTML reads or replaces an element's HTML markup.

const container = document.querySelector(".course-list"); container.innerHTML = `

Frontend Engineering

`;
This is useful for intentionally generating structured markup.
However, inserting untrusted user content through innerHTML can create Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.
Never assume that text from a form, local storage, URL parameter, or backend response is safe HTML.
For ordinary text content, prefer textContent.
const image = document.querySelector("img"); image.setAttribute( "alt", "Frontend engineering course" );
The classList API makes class manipulation easier.
This is useful for menus, tabs, dialogs, and interactive components.
JavaScript can create new DOM elements.

const card = document.createElement("article"); card.classList.add("course-card"); const title = document.createElement("h2"); title.textContent = "Frontend Engineering"; card.appendChild(title); document.body.appendChild(card);
This constructs an element tree programmatically.
The DOM provides insertion methods such as:
These make DOM construction easier than manually manipulating HTML strings.
The element is removed from its parent.
Some HTML attributes correspond to DOM properties, but the two concepts are not always identical.
The value attribute generally represents the initial/default value.
The value property represents the current input value.
For form manipulation, using the appropriate DOM properties is often necessary.
<form id="course-form"> <label for="course-name">Course Name</label> <input id="course-name" name="courseName" required > <button type="submit"> Add Course </button> </form>

const form = document.querySelector("#course-form"); form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => { event.preventDefault(); const formData = new FormData(form); const courseName = formData.get("courseName"); console.log(courseName); });
The FormData interface makes it convenient to collect form field values.
The browser has several useful document lifecycle events.
DOMContentLoaded fires after the initial HTML document has been parsed and deferred scripts and module scripts have executed.
It does not wait for every image and external resource to finish loading.
The load event is associated with completion of the document and its dependent resources.
A script using a module or an appropriately configured deferred script often does not need an additional DOMContentLoaded wrapper for basic DOM access.
Events represent actions or occurrences that JavaScript can respond to.
const button = document.querySelector("#start"); button.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Learning started"); });
The event listener receives an event object.
Identifies the element whose listener is currently executing.
Indicates whether the event's default action has been prevented.
Other properties depend on the event type.
The input event is triggered when an applicable form control's value is changed through user interaction.
The change event fires when a control's value change is committed according to that control's behavior.
The difference matters when building live search or filtering systems.
Listeners can be removed with removeEventListener().
function handleClick() { console.log("Clicked"); } button.addEventListener("click", handleClick); button.removeEventListener("click", handleClick);
The same function reference must be supplied for the corresponding listener registration.
An AbortController can also help manage event listener cleanup.
const controller = new AbortController(); button.addEventListener( "click", handleClick, { signal: controller.signal } ); controller.abort();
This removes the listener registered with that signal.
Build an interactive course list using the DOM.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — Event Propagation, Delegation and Browser Interaction

blocks.text: When an event occurs on an element, the event system may propagate that event through the document's event path.
This is important when building nested interactive interfaces.
During capturing, the event travels from relevant outer ancestors toward the target.
Listeners can be registered during this phase.
The true option registers the listener in the capturing phase.
After reaching the target, many events propagate back through ancestor elements during the bubbling phase.

const parent = document.querySelector("#parent"); const child = document.querySelector("#child"); parent.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Parent clicked"); }); child.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("Button clicked"); });
This is an example of event bubbling.
Not every event bubbles, so developers should consult the relevant event behavior.
The stopPropagation() method prevents an event from continuing through its propagation path.
The parent listener will not run for that propagated event through the stopped path.
Avoid using this indiscriminately because it may interfere with other components or delegated event listeners.
The preventDefault() method prevents a cancelable event's default browser action.
const link = document.querySelector("a"); link.addEventListener("click", (event) => { event.preventDefault(); console.log("Navigation prevented"); });
This is useful when the application implements custom behavior.
It does not stop event propagation.
The defaultPrevented property can be checked by later event listeners.
Event delegation uses event propagation to manage events for multiple child elements through a common ancestor.
Instead of attaching separate listeners to every button:

const list = document.querySelector("#course-list"); list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { const button = event.target.closest("button[data-course]"); if (!button || !list.contains(button)) { return; } console.log(button.dataset.course); });
The parent handles clicks originating from matching descendants.
Event delegation is especially helpful when:
It can reduce listener setup and simplify interactions.
However, it should only be used when event bubbling and the relevant event type support the intended pattern.
9.8 Understanding Event Target vs Current Target
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { console.log("Target:", event.target); console.log("Current Target:", event.currentTarget); });
If the user clicks a button inside the list:
currentTarget is the list element that owns the listener.
This distinction is essential for event delegation.

const taskList = document.querySelector("#task-list"); function addTask(title) { const item = document.createElement("li"); const button = document.createElement("button"); button.type = "button"; button.textContent = title; button.classList.add("complete-task"); item.append(button); taskList.append(item); } taskList.addEventListener("click", (event) => { if (event.target.matches(".complete-task")) { event.target.closest("li").classList.toggle("completed"); } });
The listener continues to work for newly created buttons because the event is handled by the persistent ancestor.
Pointer events provide a unified mechanism for handling input from:
const card = document.querySelector(".card"); card.addEventListener("pointerdown", (event) => { console.log("Pointer type:", event.pointerType); });
Pointer events are useful for advanced interaction patterns.
They should not be used to replace semantic controls or keyboard support.
JavaScript provides keyboard events such as:
Avoid building custom keyboard shortcuts that interfere with browser or assistive-technology functionality.
Where custom interactions are necessary, document them and provide alternative controls.
JavaScript allows applications to create custom events.
const event = new CustomEvent("courseCompleted", { detail: { courseId: 101 } }); document.dispatchEvent(event);
Custom events help different application components communicate without requiring direct references to one another.
They do not automatically provide accessible announcements. User-visible state changes still need appropriate accessibility behavior.
JavaScript applications often interact with host-provided browser APIs.
Used to communicate with network resources.
Used to manage browser navigation history in appropriate applications.
Used to interact with the clipboard where permissions and browser requirements allow.
Used to access location information with user permission.
These APIs provide capabilities beyond the ECMAScript language itself.
Build an interactive course-management interface demonstrating:
Errors occur when software encounters conditions that prevent the intended operation from completing.
Professional applications must handle errors without unexpectedly crashing or leaving users confused.
JavaScript errors can occur because of:
Error handling is a fundamental software engineering responsibility.
These occur when JavaScript code violates language syntax.
The missing closing parenthesis causes a syntax error.
The affected script or module may fail to parse.
These occur while code is executing.
This produces a TypeError because a property is accessed on null.
The program executes but produces an incorrect result.
function calculateAverage(a, b) { return a + b / 2; }
Logical errors can be harder to detect because the code may not produce an exception.
JavaScript provides several built-in error types.
Occurs when an operation cannot be performed on a value of the required type or structure.
Occurs when an invalid variable reference is made.
Occurs when a value is outside an allowed range for an operation.
Relates to invalid URI encoding or decoding operations.
These error types help developers identify the nature of a problem.
The try...catch structure allows code to handle thrown exceptions.
try { const result = JSON.parse("{invalid json}"); console.log(result); } catch (error) { console.error("Unable to parse JSON:", error); }
The error transfers control to the catch block.
This prevents an otherwise unhandled exception from propagating through that call path.

finally executes after the try and catch processing completes, regardless of whether an exception occurred.
try { console.log("Processing"); } catch (error) { console.error(error); } finally { console.log("Operation finished"); }
It is useful for cleanup operations that must occur regardless of success or failure.
A return statement or thrown error inside finally can affect normal control flow, so avoid using those patterns without a clear reason.
Developers can create and throw errors.
function enrolStudent(student) { if (!student.name) { throw new Error("Student name is required."); } return "Enrolment processed"; }
A calling function can handle the error.
Use clear error messages that help identify the problem without exposing sensitive implementation details to users.
class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(message) { super(message); this.name = "ValidationError"; } }
function validateCourse(title) { if (!title) { throw new ValidationError( "Course title is required." ); } }
Custom errors help distinguish different failure categories.
Rejected promises can be handled using try...catch.

async function loadCourses() { try { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error( `Request failed with status ${response.status}` ); } const courses = await response.json(); return courses; } catch (error) { console.error("Course loading failed:", error); throw error; } }
Throwing the error again allows callers to decide how to handle the failure.
Do not silently swallow unexpected errors.
A failed network request can have several causes:
The Fetch API does not reject automatically for ordinary HTTP error statuses.
For example, an HTTP 404 response can still produce a fulfilled fetch Promise.
The console API provides useful debugging tools.
console.log("Normal message"); console.warn("Potential problem"); console.error("An error occurred"); console.info("Information");
console.time("calculation"); let total = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { total += i; } console.timeEnd("calculation");
These tools are useful during development.
Avoid leaving sensitive data or unnecessary debugging output in production code.
Browser developer tools allow code execution to be paused.
A breakpoint helps identify the point at which program behavior becomes incorrect.
Changing random lines without understanding the problem usually creates more debugging work.
Source maps connect generated or bundled JavaScript back to its original source files.
They are useful when working with build tools that transform, bundle, or minify code.
Without source maps, debugging a production bundle may require navigating compressed or generated JavaScript.
Development tools can use source maps to provide a more readable debugging experience.
Create a small application that deliberately includes:
For each issue, document the cause, observed behavior, debugging process, and correction.

sections.title: LESSON 11 — Object-Oriented and Functional JavaScript Patterns

blocks.text: A programming paradigm is an approach to organizing and designing software.
Organizes application behavior and state around objects.
Emphasizes functions, predictable transformations, composition, and controlled state changes.
Objects represent entities with properties and behavior.
const student = { name: "Alex", course: "JavaScript", study() { return `${this.name} is studying ${this.course}`; } };
The object contains both data and a method.
Before class syntax became common, constructor functions were used to create objects with shared prototypes.
function Student(name, course) { this.name = name; this.course = course; } const firstStudent = new Student("Alex", "JavaScript");
The new operator creates a new object and invokes the constructor with that object as its this value.
Constructor functions are still useful when understanding JavaScript's prototype-based object model and existing codebases.
Objects can have another object as their prototype.
Property lookup can follow this prototype chain.
const person = { greet() { return "Hello"; } }; const student = Object.create(person); student.name = "Alex"; console.log(student.greet());
The student object can access greet() through its prototype chain.
The method does not need to be duplicated directly on the student object.
When a property is not found directly on an object, JavaScript looks for it on the object's prototype.
If necessary, this lookup continues through additional prototypes.
This continues until the property is found or the chain reaches null.
Understanding prototype lookup explains how built-in objects share methods.
For example, arrays can use methods inherited through their prototype chain.
JavaScript provides class syntax for organizing constructor-based object creation and prototype methods.

class Student { constructor(name, course) { this.name = name; this.course = course; } introduce() { return `${this.name} studies ${this.course}`; } } const student = new Student("Alex", "JavaScript"); console.log(student.introduce());
JavaScript classes are built on the language's prototype system.
They provide a clearer syntax for defining constructor behavior and instance methods.
The constructor() method initializes newly created instances.
class Course { constructor(title, duration) { this.title = title; this.duration = duration; } }
The constructor runs when the class is instantiated with new.
Methods defined in a class body are generally placed on the class prototype.
class Course { constructor(title) { this.title = title; } getTitle() { return this.title; } }
This allows instances to share the same method implementation.
Static methods belong to the class rather than individual instances.
class Course { static platformName() { return "PrepSpaces"; } } console.log(Course.platformName());
Calling the method on an ordinary instance is not equivalent to calling it on the class.
Static methods are useful for operations associated with a class as a whole.
Inheritance allows one class to extend another class.

class User { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } login() { return `${this.name} logged in`; } } class Student extends User { constructor(name, course) { super(name); this.course = course; } study() { return `${this.name} is studying ${this.course}`; } }
The Student class inherits functionality from User.
The super() call invokes the parent constructor.
A subclass can provide its own implementation of an inherited method.
class User { getRole() { return "User"; } } class Admin extends User { getRole() { return "Administrator"; } }
The Admin method overrides the inherited method for instances of that class.
Encapsulation organizes internal object state and behavior behind a controlled interface.
JavaScript supports private class fields using the # syntax.
class BankAccount { #balance = 0; deposit(amount) { if (amount <= 0) { throw new Error("Invalid amount"); } this.#balance += amount; } getBalance() { return this.#balance; } }
The private field cannot be accessed through ordinary external property access.
This provides a way to protect internal implementation details.
Getters and setters provide controlled property access.
class Student { constructor(name) { this._name = name; } get name() { return this._name; } set name(value) { if (!value) { throw new Error("Name is required"); } this._name = value; } }
const student = new Student("Alex"); console.log(student.name); student.name = "Sam";
The getter and setter make the property appear like a normal property while allowing custom behavior.
The underscore in _name is only a naming convention; it does not make the property private.
Composition combines smaller behavior units to create larger functionality.

const canStudy = { study() { console.log("Studying"); } }; const canCompleteCourse = { completeCourse() { console.log("Course completed"); } }; function createStudent(name) { return { name, ...canStudy, ...canCompleteCourse }; }
Composition is frequently preferable when deep inheritance hierarchies would make an application difficult to understand.
Functional programming emphasizes functions as the primary units for organizing transformations and computation.
Produces the same output for the same inputs.
Does not cause externally observable side effects.
function calculateTotal(price, tax) { return price + tax; }
Calling the function with the same arguments produces the same result.
let total = 0; function addToTotal(value) { total += value; }
Pure functions are easier to test and reason about.
Immutability means avoiding unwanted changes to existing data.
This approach is especially useful when managing application state.
It can reduce unexpected changes caused by shared references.
Remember that spread-based copies are shallow.
A higher-order function accepts another function or returns one.
function applyDiscount(price, discountFunction) { return discountFunction(price); } const discount = price => price * 0.9; console.log( applyDiscount(1000, discount) );
This separates the process from the specific discount calculation.
Composition combines smaller functions into larger operations.
const trimText = text => text.trim(); const toLowerCase = text => text.toLowerCase(); const normalize = text => toLowerCase(trimText(text)); console.log(normalize(" JAVASCRIPT "));
This can improve testability and reuse.
Imperative programming describes the steps required to achieve an outcome.
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const doubled = []; for (const number of numbers) { if (number > 2) { doubled.push(number * 2); } }
Declarative programming describes the transformation more directly.
Choose the one that makes the implementation easiest to understand and maintain.
Modern JavaScript applications frequently combine both approaches.
For example, a task application may use objects to represent tasks and pure functions to filter and sort them.

sections.title: LESSON 12 — Memory Management and JavaScript Performance Fundamentals

blocks.text: Applications create, modify, and retain data during execution.
Every JavaScript application needs memory for:
As an application becomes more complex, unnecessary memory retention can reduce performance and create memory leaks.
Developers must understand how memory is allocated, used, retained, and released.
When JavaScript creates values, the engine manages the necessary memory.
const name = "Alex"; const student = { name: "Alex", age: 22 };
The engine stores and manages the relevant values.
Developers generally do not manually allocate or release individual JavaScript memory locations.
Instead, the engine manages memory through its internal memory-management mechanisms.
A simplified memory model commonly describes two areas:
Associated with function execution and temporary execution state.
Associated with dynamically allocated objects and other values.

The exact memory representation of JavaScript values is engine-dependent. Not every primitive must physically occupy a stack location, and JavaScript specifications do not mandate one universal stack-and-heap implementation.
JavaScript engines automatically reclaim memory that is no longer needed.
This process is known as garbage collection.
Modern engines commonly use reachability-based garbage collection.
If an object can no longer be reached through relevant references, it can generally be considered eligible for collection.
After removing the reference, the original object may become eligible for garbage collection if no other references to it remain.
Garbage collection timing is controlled by the engine.
Developers cannot assume that memory is released immediately after a reference disappears.
An object can remain in memory while it remains reachable from relevant roots.
As long as student remains reachable, its object remains available.
If an active closure, event listener, or another object still references it, removing one variable may not make it collectible.
A memory leak occurs when memory that is no longer needed remains retained.
A global reference can retain a large data structure for the lifetime of the page.
Long-lived event targets can retain references through registered callbacks.
function setup() { const largeData = new Array(100000).fill("data"); window.addEventListener("resize", () => { console.log(largeData.length); }); }
If the listener is never removed, this environment may continue retaining that data.
A better design should remove the listener or use appropriate listener lifecycle management.
Repeated timers can continue running after a component or page feature is no longer needed.
Clear it when no longer needed:
JavaScript references to removed DOM nodes can keep those nodes and related data reachable.
Removing an element from the document does not necessarily make every object associated with it immediately collectible.
Long-lived functions may retain references to large data structures.
Closures are not inherently memory leaks, but their lifetime should be considered.
A WeakMap associates values with object keys using weak references to the keys.
const metadata = new WeakMap(); let courseElement = document.createElement("div"); metadata.set(courseElement, { courseId: 101 }); console.log(metadata.get(courseElement));
WeakMaps do not prevent their object keys from becoming garbage-collectible solely because they appear as keys in the WeakMap.
WeakSets similarly hold object references weakly.
They are useful for certain metadata and object-lifecycle patterns.
They are not iterable and cannot be used like normal Map or Set collections.
Performance also depends on how much work an algorithm performs as data grows.
Big O notation describes an algorithm's asymptotic complexity.
Comparing every pair using nested loops
A direct indexed lookup is commonly treated as O(1).
Iterating through every value is O(n).
Nested iteration can produce O(n²) behavior.
for (const first of numbers) { for (const second of numbers) { console.log(first, second); } }
Understanding algorithmic complexity helps developers avoid inefficient data processing.
DOM manipulation can affect browser performance.
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { const item = document.createElement("li"); item.textContent = `Task ${i}`; document.querySelector("#task-list").appendChild(item); }
A document fragment can help organize batch insertion:

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment(); for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { const item = document.createElement("li"); item.textContent = `Task ${i}`; fragment.appendChild(item); } document.querySelector("#task-list").appendChild(fragment);
This creates the elements in a detached fragment before inserting them.
Modern browsers optimize DOM operations in several ways, so batching is not a guarantee of a specific performance improvement in every situation. Measure before optimizing.
A long-running JavaScript task can block the main thread.
For example, a large synchronous calculation can make the interface appear unresponsive.
Moving suitable computation into a Web Worker.
Debouncing ensures that a function is executed after a period of inactivity.

function debounce(callback, delay) { let timer; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => { callback(...args); }, delay); }; } const searchCourses = debounce((value) => { console.log("Searching:", value); }, 300);
The callback runs after the user stops triggering the function for the specified period.
Throttling limits how frequently a function executes.
function throttle(callback, delay) { let lastExecution = 0; return (...args) => { const now = Date.now(); if (now - lastExecution >= delay) { lastExecution = now; callback(...args); } }; }
This is a basic throttling implementation.
Production implementations may also need leading and trailing execution options.
requestAnimationFrame() schedules a callback to run before a browser rendering opportunity.
function animate() { console.log("Animation frame"); requestAnimationFrame(animate); } requestAnimationFrame(animate);
This is useful for JavaScript-driven visual updates.
For many standard animations, CSS transitions and keyframes are preferable because the browser can optimize them without requiring continuous JavaScript execution.
Browser developer tools provide several useful performance-analysis capabilities.
Provides automated audits covering selected areas such as performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.
Automated results help identify opportunities but should be interpreted alongside real testing.
Clear timers when their purpose ends.
Use Web Workers for suitable heavy computations.
Create a JavaScript application that demonstrates:
Browser Performance and Memory panel inspection.
Prepare a short performance report describing the bottlenecks found and the improvements implemented.

sections.title: PRACTICAL PROJECT — Build an Interactive Task-Management Application Using Vanilla JavaScript

blocks.text: Build a complete task-management application using HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript.

The project must demonstrate the ability to apply JavaScript programming fundamentals, data structures, DOM manipulation, event handling, modular architecture, form validation, error handling, and browser storage.
The application should work without React, Vue, Angular, or another frontend framework.
The objective is to build an actual working application, not a collection of isolated JavaScript exercises.
Users should be able to create tasks.

const task = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title: "Learn JavaScript", description: "Complete DOM manipulation lessons.", priority: "high", dueDate: "2026-12-01", completed: false, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() };
Validate the required fields before creating the task.
Display all tasks in an organized interface.
The user should be able to identify task information quickly.
Allow users to modify existing tasks.
Do not create a duplicate task when editing an existing one.
Allow users to remove unwanted tasks.
Include a suitable confirmation mechanism where necessary.
Allow users to mark tasks as completed or incomplete.
The application should update the visual state and task statistics.
The filters should work without creating duplicate task records.
Users should be able to search using task titles and descriptions.

Use browser local storage to preserve task information across page reloads.
const storedTasks = localStorage.getItem("tasks"); const tasks = storedTasks ? JSON.parse(storedTasks) : [];
Production-quality handling must also account for malformed stored JSON and unavailable storage.

function loadTasks() { try { const stored = localStorage.getItem("tasks"); if (!stored) { return []; } const parsed = JSON.parse(stored); if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) { return []; } return parsed; } catch (error) { console.error("Unable to load saved tasks:", error); return []; } }
Store only information appropriate for browser-side persistence.
Do not store passwords, authentication tokens, or sensitive personal information as ordinary local-storage values.
localStorage is browser-side storage, not a secure database or a multi-user synchronization system.

After completing this module, students should be able to write JavaScript beyond isolated examples and develop structured application logic.
They should understand how JavaScript executes, how values and references behave, how functions retain scope, how data is processed, and how modules organize larger applications.

They should also be comfortable manipulating the DOM, handling browser interactions, managing asynchronous operations, debugging errors, applying programming paradigms, and identifying performance problems.

The final objective is to build an interactive application in vanilla JavaScript with clear data models, predictable state updates, reusable functions, proper error handling, and maintainable module boundaries.
Expected outcome: Students should be able to build a functional browser-based application using JavaScript without depending on a frontend framework.
